extracted.intended_audience: photographers and amateur scientific experimenters (photographic technicians, artisans, and laboratory practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical how-to for preparing gelatine-silver photographic plates (emulsion preparation, precipitation, washing, coating and drying) aimed at photographers and technicians. Includes related practical procedures for vitreous picture reproduction and a laboratory method for preparing hydrogen sulphide from coal-gas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of silver nitrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Nitrate of silver is supplied in three principal conditions: ordinary crystallized salt (often yellowish and containing free acid), fused nitrate or 'lunar caustic' (alkaline to test paper), and recrystallized silver nitrate (colorless, transparent, perfectly neutral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inexperienced operators, use recrystallized silver nitrate. Prepare a solution of recrystallized silver nitrate in distilled water containing 1¼ ounces of the salt in every 12 ounces of solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of soluble bromide (ammonium vs potassium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several bromides may be used (ammonium, potassium, barium, zinc), but ammonium bromide is unstable, becomes acid on keeping, varies in bromine content, and has a destructive action on gelatine causing pink fog and frilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer potassium bromide: it is stable, obtainable pure, constant in composition, and has no appreciable destructive action on gelatine. Prepare a potassium bromide solution containing 1 ounce of salt in every 12 ounces of solution; if the solution is slightly alkaline or neutral, faintly acidify with hydrochloric acid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of gelatine
rubrics_metrics.description: Gelatine quality varies; to secure uniform results the only method is to buy several small samples, trial each by making an emulsion, and stock the best-performing sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For those who won't test, use equal quantities of Nelson's No. 1 and 'X opaque' (as recommended by Captain Abney). Practical working quantity: allow 1¼ ounces of gelatine to soak and melt to yield about 6 ounces bulk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions and initial mixing of emulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: To prepare the emulsion take equal bulks of the silver nitrate and potassium bromide solutions and heat them in a water bath; separately prepare hot water with gelatine (½ ounce gelatine per 12 ounces water).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring all to about 180°F; add small portions alternately (a little bromide then a little silver) through a fine-orifice funnel while swirling. Maintain bromide in excess during mixing (experienced workers may follow Abney's method of keeping silver in excess). A correctly mixed emulsion appears orange/red by transmitted light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling (ripening) of emulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Once mixed, the emulsion is kept at the boiling point for forty-five minutes (one portion can be 'stewed' while another is left unboiled for demonstration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boiling causes silver-bromide molecules to aggregate into larger particles and increases sensitiveness. The presence of excess potassium bromide (not heat alone) is the prime cause of this ripening; a washed emulsion without excess niter/bromide will not ripen even when boiled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of excess potassium bromide on ripening speed
rubrics_metrics.description: The time for an emulsion to acquire maximum sensitiveness depends on the excess of potassium bromide present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table given: 0.2 grain per ounce → no increase after six hours; 2.0 grains per ounce → ~½ hour; 20.0 grains per ounce → 7 minutes. Use this to control ripening time by adjusting KBr excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing cause of ripening (experimental control)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine which component causes ripening, prepare washed emulsion (removing niter and excess KBr) and add back separately niter or KBr before boiling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: samples with added KBr ripen; with niter they do not—demonstrating importance of KBr excess. This experimental control is recommended to understand and reproduce ripening behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precipitation and daylight-safe handling (bichromate + HCl)
rubrics_metrics.description: For subsequent handling in daylight, precipitate gelatine (carrying silver bromide) by adding potassium bichromate and a little hydrochloric acid to liberate chromic acid which precipitates gelatine and destroys light-sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add, for every 6 ounces of mixed emulsion, 1 ounce of a saturated cold solution of potassium bichromate, swirl, then add a few drops of dilute (1:8) HCl; allow a minute or two, pour off clear supernatant, and transfer clot to the dark room for washing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washing and redissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: After precipitation, wash the pellicle until wash water shows no trace of colour; for large quantities use a fine muslin filter, for small quantities use decantation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After thorough washing, dissolve the pellicle by immersing the vessel in a water bath, then add the remaining gelatine and make up the bulk with alcohol and water as prescribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final composition, alcohol content, and filtration
rubrics_metrics.description: Final emulsion finishing: after redissolving and adding remaining gelatine, adjust volume and add alcohol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the quantities given, make up to 30 ounces with 3 ounces of alcohol and water; filter the emulsion through a funnel containing a pellet of cotton wool to remove impurities before coating plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plate coating procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Method for coating a glass plate with emulsion: place plate on a leveled block, pour emulsion down a glass rod and spread with a horizontally held rod, then transfer plate to a leveled slab for the emulsion to set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once set, place the plate in a drying box. This yields plates suitable for landscape work; further operations (not fully detailed here) are required to obtain plates of the highest sensitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ammonium bromide anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Ammonium bromide is unstable and has deleterious effects on gelatin emulsions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ammonium bromide as it tends to acidify on storage, vary in bromine content, and cause 'pink fog' and frilling on plates—common source of defects in many published formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chromic acid (from bichromate + HCl) to stop light action
rubrics_metrics.description: Chromic acid liberated from bichromate + acid precipitates gelatin and destroys the action of light on silver bromide so that subsequent operations may be carried out in daylight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows safe transfer of precipitated emulsion to the dark room for washing; employ only until washing removes chromic residues (wash until clear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for achieving highest sensitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The boiling/steaming (ripening) procedure described yields plates of very good quality suitable for landscape; attaining the highest degree of sensitiveness requires a further operation beyond this basic procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the distinction: the given method is adequate for many uses, but additional sensitizing steps (not specified in this abstract) are needed for maximum speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original drawing preparation for glass pictorial reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Original drawings/images should be well executed and drawn on white or preferably bluish paper similar to ordinary drawing paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a high-quality original improves fidelity of the reproduced vitrifiable image on glass or other polished surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass cutting and placement prior to coating
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut sheets of glass to suit the shades/panels indicated by lead lines; place each cut sheet on the reverse side of the prepared drawing (paper made transparent with petroleum) with the coated side to contact the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work one panel at a time for large stained-glass windows; petroleum-saturated paper fixes outlines and gives vigor to the paper's dark tones for transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitizing solution composition for pictures on glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitizing solution: saturated bichromate of ammonia in water; separately dissolve 5 grammes powdered dextrin or glucose in 100 grammes water; to either solution add 10% of the bichromate solution and filter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coat the glass on the side that will contact the paper with as thin and uniform a layer as possible; a second brush can assist in making the coating perfectly even. Perform coating in a dark room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying conditions for sensitized glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Dry coated glass sheets in a small hot chamber at 50–60°C (120–140°F) laid on a wire grating 35 cm above the bottom; do not introduce the glass until required temperature is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few seconds are sufficient to dry each sheet; place dried sheets where heat is less intense. Avoid overdrying at high temperatures (>25°C) because sheets may 'instantly metallize' when exposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure time and temperature guidance for glass reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure time depends on light and temperature: in fine, cloudless weather at 16–18°C (60–64°F) allow 12–15 minutes; in dark weather allow 30–50 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If temperature >25°C, keep sheets cool and less dried; if <5°C, keep sheets warm and do not expose to open air—keep behind a window at ~14–18°C. Always check exposure by test: apply vitrifiable color to a test piece and judge adhesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure assessment by vitrifiable color adhesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine correct exposure by taking a test piece and applying vitrifiable color: the powder should adhere only to shady/deeper tones and not to fully exposed areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If color adheres only slightly to dark/shady portions, exposure was too long (recommence). If color adheres too well (even to highlights), exposure was insufficient—close frame and continue exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing bichromate coating and fixing image for vitrification
rubrics_metrics.description: After developing with vitrifiable color, dip the glass in a bath composed of 30–40 grammes nitric acid per 1,000 grammes wood-spirit (photographic solvent) to remove the bichromate coating and allow the color to adhere to the glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change the bath when it becomes yellowish. The bath also renders light parts pure and easy to retouch; afterward apply colored enamels and heat as in ordinary glass painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to other substrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Process applicable to marble, wood, stone, lava, canvas prepared for oil painting, earthenware, and enameled or pure iron, with the same steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-immersible substrates, pour the nitric-wood-spirit liquid over the object placed inclined, rather than dipping the object into the bath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrogen sulphide preparation overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Hydrogen sulphide may be prepared simply and sufficiently pure for ordinary analytical purposes by passing coal-gas through boiling sulphur; coal-gas contains 40–50% hydrogen which is converted to H2S while other constituents remain unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces H2S appropriate for precipitating metallic sulphides in routine laboratory work; no further purification is necessary for ordinary analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus design for H2S from coal-gas
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparatus: a retort containing sulphur with a bent glass tube perforated near the closed end and dipping into the sulphur; the gas inlet is connected to the perforated tube, the retort neck (inclined upward) connects to a wash bottle, then to a receiving flask and an aspirator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perforations in the tube are made by piercing softened glass. The neck should be inclined to allow condensed sulphur to flow back. Use caoutchouc tubing for connections and an aspirator to draw the gas through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for producing H2S from coal-gas
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce ~1 pound of sulphur into the retort and heat to boiling; turn on aspirator and draw a current of coal-gas through the boiling sulphur; the hydrogen in the coal-gas reacts to form hydrogen sulphide which is washed and collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formed H2S is washed in the wash bottle (B), passes into the receiving flask (F) and then to the aspirator (A). The other coal-gas constituents (methane, CO, olefines) are not affected and do not interfere with precipitations of metallic sulphides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding efficiency losses in dynamo machines
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-conceived dynamo must avoid losses by unnecessary wire resistance, by Foucault (eddy) currents, and by induced currents in the rotating armature to realize high efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these losses are avoided, as much as 90% or more of the power communicated to the machine may be realized as electric energy; reconversion to mechanical energy can be accomplished with similarly small loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical condition for power transmission between two dynamos
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum yield is obtained when two dynamo machines of similar construction rotate nearly the same speed, but that condition yields minimum transmitted force. Practically it is best to give the primary such proportions as to produce a current of the same magnitude but with 50% greater electromotive force than the secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By adopting such an arrangement, as much as 50% of the power imparted to the primary could be practically received from the secondary machine at a distance of several miles. Professor Silvanus Thompson's graphical method may be used to prove these laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric power unit recommendation (watt and joule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion to add the watt and the joule to electrical units to complete the chain connecting electrical with mechanical energy (746 watts = 1 horse-power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The watt is convenient for expressing the effective power of a dynamo and for giving precise ideas of number of lights and engine power necessary. Demonstrated instrument: the watt meter with two coils (one representing amperes, one volts) whose joint attractive action reads volt-amperes or watts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of electric propulsion applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric propulsion is sufficiently advanced for practical success under suitable circumstances such as suburban tramways, elevated lines, and lines through tunnels (e.g., Metropolitan and District Railways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include reduced weight of engines on moving vehicles and absence of combustion products; the lecturer does not advocate electric propulsion in competition with locomotive engines for main lines. For tramways within populous districts, insulation of conductors is a difficulty—secondary batteries under seats are an alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary battery permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns existed that local action and sulphate of lead formation would destroy secondary batteries; experiments show the action depends on the alternative composition and decomposition of sulphate of lead, making it supportive rather than destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports the practical permanence and usefulness of Faure/Sellon/Volckmar type lead-acid secondary batteries for storing energy in conjunction with dynamo machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tramway implementation details (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several mechanical/electrical implementations were described: Siemens' Berlin exhibition arrangement using a central insulated rail, the Lichterfelde line using insulated sleepers for both rails as conductors, and the Portrush–Bush Mills line using uninsulated rails joined as return with a T iron insulated on standards for feed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include line lengths, power ratings (e.g., Lichterfelde: 2,500 yards, 9,000 watts = 12 HP), operational experience (continuous operation since 16 May 1881), and Board of Trade speed limits (e.g., 10 mph) relevant to design choices.
